Emotions

Is it bad to be bored?

Boredom is uncomfortable, but it is a useful signal: it tells us what we are doing is not fulfilling.

With a phone always at hand, boredom has almost disappeared from our lives. A second's wait is enough to bring out the screen. But is being bored so bad?

An uncomfortable emotion

In a 2014 study, Timothy Wilson and colleagues left people alone in a room for six to fifteen minutes with nothing to do but think. Within reach was a button that gave them a small electric shock they had earlier said they would pay to avoid. Two in three men and one in four women gave themselves at least one shock. Being bored was so unpleasant that they preferred pain.

The researchers James Danckert and John Eastwood describe boredom as the feeling of wanting to engage in something satisfying and being unable to. That is why it is a signal: it pushes us to look for something else.

Its useful side

Some studies suggest that after a boring task people are more creative: in a 2014 experiment, those who had copied numbers from a phone book came up with more original uses for plastic cups. Other studies find no effect, but there is agreement that letting the mind wander at times helps us plan and connect ideas.

We would rather have a shock

In 2014, Timothy Wilson and colleagues asked people to spend between six and fifteen minutes alone in a room, with no phone or anything to do, just their thoughts. They had the option of giving themselves a small electric shock that they had earlier said they would pay to avoid. Two thirds of the men and a quarter of the women gave themselves at least one. Being alone with one's own mind is, for many, more uncomfortable than we imagine.

Chronic boredom

Some people get bored much more easily than others. Boredom proneness is associated with more impulsivity, substance use, gambling, overeating and depressive symptoms. It has also been linked to ADHD. The answer is not to fill every minute, but to find activities that offer a challenge of the right size and mean something to the person.

What usually helps

  • Tolerate stretches without stimulation, for example while waiting or on a walk without headphones.
  • Listen to what boredom is saying: if it appears a lot at work or in your studies, perhaps challenge, meaning or variety are missing.
  • Look for absorbing activities, hard enough to require attention.
Constant boredom, together with a loss of interest in everything, can be a symptom of depression. If so, it is worth seeking advice.

References

  1. Wilson, T. D. et al. (2014). Just think: the challenges of the disengaged mind. Science, 345(6192), 75–77.
  2. Danckert, J. y Eastwood, J. D. (2020). Out of My Skull: The Psychology of Boredom. Harvard University Press.
  3. Mann, S. y Cadman, R. (2014). Does being bored make us more creative? Creativity Research Journal, 26(2), 165–173.
  4. Wilson, T. D. et al. (2014). Just think: the challenges of the disengaged mind. Science, 345, 75–77.
  5. Eastwood, J. D., Frischen, A., Fenske, M. J. y Smilek, D. (2012). The unengaged mind: defining boredom in terms of attention. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 7(5), 482–495.
